titleText.es: Mierda. No sólo no me lo instaló, sino que me suturó una pegatina en el brazo diciendo
titleText.en: Damn. Not only did he not install it, he sutured a 'Vista-Ready' sticker onto my arm.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive title attribute is genuinely truncated after diciendo because unescaped nested quotation marks terminate the HTML attribute; this field preserves that archive value exactly. The official English title text is complete and copied exactly. The raster's two USB labels remain explicit non-Spanish technical exclusions, while the surrounding Spanish technical vocabulary stays clickable.

regions.labelEs: MIENTRAS ME ESTÉ OPERANDO, ¿PUEDE IMPLANTARME ESTO EN EL BRAZO?

applications.explanationEn: Mientras introduces the requested future situation, me identifies the patient, and esté operando uses the special pending-action form.
Esté supplies the needed form of estar, while operando gives the ongoing surgical action with its -ando ending.
Puede makes the polite formal request, while implantarme keeps implantar in its unchanged dictionary form.
Me attaches to the end of implantar and identifies the speaker as the person receiving the implant.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the unchanged international technical acronym, not a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: TAN SOLO CONÉCTELO A ALGUNOS NERVIOS.

applications.explanationEn: Tan adds emphasis to solo, and together they limit the instruction to this supposedly simple step.
Conecte is the formal usted command of conectar.
Lo attaches to the formal command conecte, and the written accent preserves the original stress.

regions.labelEs: ... ES CONSCIENTE DE QUE ESTO NO LE PERMITIRÁ CONTROLAR DISPOSITIVOS USB, ¿NO?

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the unchanged international technical acronym, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Le identifies the formal listener, permitirá carries the future allowing action, and controlar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Permitirá keeps permitir and adds the -á future ending for one subject.

regions.labelEs: CLARO. YO SOLO QUIERO EL HARDWARE.
EL RESTO ES SOFTWARE; ESTOY SEGURO DE QUE EN ALGÚN MOMENTO HABRÁ UN PROYECTO PARA AÑADIRLE SOPORTE.

applications.explanationEn: En algún momento places the hoped-for project at an unspecified future point.
Para introduces the project's purpose, while añadirle keeps añadir in its unchanged dictionary form with le attached.
Le attaches to añadir and stands for the system receiving the new compatibility.
Añadirle marks the already understood system as the receiver, and soporte names the compatibility to be added.

regions.labelEs: AH, VEO QUE ES USUARIO DE LINUX.

applications.explanationEn: Cómo keeps its accent because it directly asks how the surgeon found out.
Lo stands for the fact just inferred and comes before the conjugated helper ha.
Ha is the present helper for one formal listener, and sabido is saber's completed-action form.

cards.promptEs: mientras + subjuntivo para una acción pendiente
cards.questionEn: How do you say “while” when the action is still pending or presented as a future possibility?
cards.answerEn: Use mientras, then put the pending action's verb in a subjunctive form.
cards.noteEn: Use ordinary present forms for a routine or established overlap, but use the subjunctive when the “while” action has not happened yet or is presented as a requested future situation. A progressive action can use a subjunctive form of estar plus an -ando/-iendo form.

example.en: I will write to you while you are traveling.

cards.answerEn: is; am; are (special estar helper for an ongoing action)
cards.noteEn: Esté is a subjunctive form of estar. Before an -ando or -iendo form, it helps present an ongoing action inside a pending, uncertain, or otherwise non-established situation.

example.en: Call me while I am traveling.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

example.en: I am reading.

cards.noteEn: Operando is the -ando form of operar. In a medical setting, operar means performing surgery on someone.

example.es: La cirujana está operando al paciente.
example.en: The surgeon is operating on the patient.

cards.answerEn: can you; could you (formal or polite request)
cards.noteEn: In a question to one person addressed formally as usted, ¿puede + action? can make a polite request. Puede has the same written form used for he, she, or it.

example.en: Could you open the window?

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

example.en: We can enter now.

cards.answerEn: to implant in me; to put inside my body
cards.noteEn: Implantar is the unchanged dictionary form, and me attaches to identify the speaker as the person receiving the implant.

example.es: Van a implantarme un pequeño sensor.
example.en: They are going to implant a small sensor in me.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

example.en: I want to help you.

cards.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

example.en: This is difficult.

cards.noteEn: In computing and electronics, a puerto is a physical or logical connection point. Elsewhere puerto can mean a harbor.

example.es: El portátil tiene un puerto libre.
example.en: The laptop has a free port.

cards.promptEs: puerto · hardware · software · proyecto · soporte · Linux
cards.answerEn: a Linux user treats an implanted physical computer port as useful because a future software project might eventually make it work
cards.noteEn: The patient knows that merely wiring a port to nerves cannot make the brain control devices. He still wants the hardware installed and trusts that an open-source software project will eventually add support. The surgeon recognizes this optimistic hardware-first attitude as characteristic of a Linux user; the official title text extends the joke with a Vista-Ready sticker.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; adds emphasis in tan solo (“only; just”)

cards.questionEn: How can you say “only” or “just” with a little extra emphasis?
cards.noteEn: Tan solo works as one fixed expression here. Tan does not keep its usual separate meaning “so”; the pair is similar to solamente or solo.

example.en: I have only five minutes.

cards.noteEn: Conecte is the command for one person addressed as usted, and lo stands for the masculine item being connected. Lo attaches to the command, and the written accent keeps the original stress.

example.en: Connect it to the screen.

cards.answerEn: Use the usted command form: regular -ar verbs end in -e, while regular -er and -ir verbs end in -a.
cards.noteEn: Usted is the polite or formal singular “you.” Hablar becomes hable, comer becomes coma, and escribir becomes escriba. Usted is usually left out because the command ending already shows formal address. Some common verbs are irregular, such as decir → diga.
cards.questionEn: How do you politely tell one person to do something in Spanish?

example.en: Come in, please.

cards.questionEn: Where does a short object pronoun go in a positive formal command?
cards.answerEn: Attach the pronoun to the end of the usted command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: Use the formal command first, then attach me, te, lo, la, le, nos, los, las, or les as needed. Add a written accent when required to preserve the command's original stress: conecte + lo becomes conéctelo.

example.es: Firme el documento y envíelo hoy.
example.en: Sign the document and send it today.

cards.answerEn: to; introduces what something is connected to
cards.noteEn: After conectar, a introduces the device, network, point, or other target receiving the connection.

example.es: Conecta el cable a la batería.
example.en: Connect the cable to the battery.

cards.noteEn: Nervios can name the body's nerves. In other contexts, tener nervios or estar nervioso describes nervousness.

example.en: Nerves transmit signals.

cards.noteEn: Consciente has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns; its plural is conscientes.

example.en: I am aware of the problem.

cards.answerEn: of; links consciente to what someone is aware of
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses consciente de before the fact, issue, or situation that a person knows about. A following que can introduce a complete fact.

example.es: Soy consciente de que falta tiempo.
example.en: I am aware that time is short.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: you; marks the formal person who is allowed to do something
cards.noteEn: With permitir, le identifies one person affected by the permission. Here that person is the formally addressed listener; English normally places “you” directly before the allowed action.

example.en: The card will allow you to enter.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something allows a person to perform an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of permitir, identify the allowed person with me, te, le, nos, os, or les, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The person marker comes before a finite form of permitir. Permitir changes for the subject and time, while the allowed action remains an -ar, -er, or -ir dictionary form: la llave me permite entrar.

example.es: El permiso les permitirá trabajar aquí.
example.en: The permit will allow them to work here.

cards.noteEn: Permitirá keeps the whole dictionary form permitir and adds -á for one future subject or formal listener.

example.es: El pase permitirá abrir la puerta.
example.en: The pass will allow the door to be opened.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

example.en: Marta will call tomorrow.

cards.noteEn: Controlar is the unchanged dictionary form. For machinery or devices, it means directing how they work.

example.es: El mando sirve para controlar el motor.
example.en: The controller is used to operate the motor.

cards.noteEn: Dispositivos is the masculine plural of dispositivo, a device or piece of equipment designed for a purpose.

example.en: Turn off the electronic devices.

cards.answerEn: right?; isn't that so? (at the end of a question)
cards.noteEn: After a statement or assumption, ¿no? asks the listener to confirm it. English often uses a changing tag such as “right?”, “isn't it?”, or “don't you?”, but Spanish can use the same ¿no? after many different verbs.

example.en: You're coming tomorrow, right?

cards.answerEn: hardware; the physical parts of a computer or electronic system
cards.noteEn: Hardware is a standard technical borrowing in Spanish. It contrasts with software, the programs and instructions rather than the physical equipment.

example.es: El fallo está en el hardware.
example.en: The fault is in the hardware.

cards.noteEn: El resto names everything left after the already mentioned part has been separated out.

example.en: We will save the rest for tomorrow.

cards.answerEn: is; belongs to the stated category
cards.noteEn: Es is the present form of ser used for one person or thing. Between two naming words, it identifies or classifies the first as the second.

example.en: Chess is a game.

cards.answerEn: I am (in a state or condition)
no separate English word here; links seguro to what someone is sure about
cards.noteEn: The adjective seguro normally takes de before the thing, fact, or question that follows. English often omits a separate preposition before a who, what, or whether clause.

example.en: I am sure that he will come.

cards.answerEn: at; begins en algún momento, “at some point”
cards.noteEn: Here en introduces an indefinite point in time rather than a physical location.

example.en: We will discuss it at some point.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “at some point” without specifying when?
cards.noteEn: Algún comes before the masculine noun momento; the expression can refer to the past or future according to the verb.

example.en: We will see each other at some point.

cards.answerEn: some; some day/time (before a masculine noun)
cards.noteEn: Alguno shortens to algún directly before a masculine singular noun: algún día, algún libro.

example.en: Some neighbor will have the key.

cards.noteEn: Habrá is the future existence form of haber. It uses the irregular future stem habr- plus -á and stays singular even when what will exist is plural.

example.en: There will be more options tomorrow.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.answerEn: to add to it; to give it an added feature
cards.noteEn: Añadir is the unchanged dictionary form, and le attaches to identify the thing receiving the addition.

example.es: Queremos añadirle una función al programa.
example.en: We want to add a feature to the program.

cards.promptEs: añadir soporte a + tecnología o función
cards.questionEn: How do you say that technical compatibility is being added for something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of añadir with soporte, then introduce the technology or feature with a; a pronoun such as le can stand for it.
cards.noteEn: Añadir changes for the person and time, while soporte names the new technical compatibility. If the receiving system is already clear, attach le to an unchanged infinitive: añadirle soporte.

example.es: Van a añadir soporte a ese formato.
example.en: They are going to add support for that format.

cards.answerEn: support; technical ability to work with something
cards.noteEn: In technology, soporte can mean that a system is compatible with a device, format, or feature, not only help from a support worker.

example.es: El navegador tiene soporte para este formato.
example.en: The browser supports this format.

cards.noteEn: Ah can show that the speaker has just understood, noticed, or recognized something. Its exact English equivalent depends on tone.

example.en: Oh, yes, now I remember.

cards.noteEn: Usuario is a person who uses a service, device, or computer account. The feminine form is usuaria.

example.en: Each user has a password.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

example.en: I need a coffee cup.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

example.en: What is your name?

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

example.en: The movie—we watched it yesterday.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.noteEn: Sabido is the completed-action form of saber. With a form of haber, it describes having learned or found out something.

example.en: How did you find out?
